articles.title: In 2025, scientists brought pregnant San Francisco garter snakes to a zoo to protect their young; on November 10, officials revealed 62 zoo-raised snakes were released into the wild after genetic testing
articles.summary: A conservation initiative involving the San Francisco Zoo, federal wildlife officials and regional land managers has resulted in the first successful
articles.body: A conservation initiative involving the San Francisco Zoo, federal wildlife officials and regional land managers has resulted in the first successful release of zoo-raised San Francisco garter snakes into their natural habitat. According to an announcement by the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens on November 10, 2026, the programme has seen 62 young snakes return to the wild after being raised in captivity. The Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District and the US Fish and Wildlife Service have also highlighted the importance of the initiative in protecting the rare species. The project began in 2025, when biologists from the US Geological Survey collected pregnant female San Francisco garter snakes from a healthy wild population in a protected area managed by Midpen. The snakes were temporarily brought to the San Francisco Zoo, where they could give birth in a controlled environment.Once the young were born, the mothers were returned to their original habitat, while the zoo’s conservation team took responsibility for raising the newborns. The idea was to give the young snakes a better chance of surviving the early stages of life, when they are particularly vulnerable to predators and competition for food. This approach, known as head-starting, involves raising young wildlife in captivity until they reach a size at which their chances of surviving in the wild improve. It has been used in conservation programmes involving several threatened species, but this marks the first successful head-starting initiative for the San Francisco garter snake.Genetic testing determined where the snakes would goBefore the 62 young snakes were released, each underwent genetic testing to help conservationists decide where it would have the greatest impact. Around one-third were returned to the areas from which their mothers had been collected. The remaining snakes were distributed among other populations that needed additional individuals and greater genetic diversity.The strategy is intended to strengthen existing populations without placing excessive pressure on the healthy population that supplied the original breeding females. The release took place at carefully selected locations across San Mateo County, California. Authorities have deliberately withheld the exact sites to protect the animals from illegal collection, road accidents and potential exposure to disease.Why the San Francisco garter snake needs protectionThe San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia) is a distinctive reptile found naturally only on the San Francisco Peninsula, primarily in San Mateo County and parts of northern Santa Cruz County. Recognisable by its striking combination of blue-green, black and red-orange markings, it is considered one of North America’s most visually distinctive snakes.However, its restricted geographical range has made the species particularly vulnerable. It was listed as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act on March 11, 1967, making it one of the earliest species to receive federal protection under the legislation. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service, habitat destruction, fragmentation, drought, reduced food availability and illegal collection continue to threaten its survival.The snakes also depend on healthy wetland ecosystems and prey on California red-legged frogs, another threatened species. Conservationists have therefore been working on habitat restoration alongside the breeding programme, improving wetland conditions and helping reconnect isolated wildlife populations.More than 130 baby snakes are being raised for the next releaseThe latest release is only the beginning of a longer recovery programme. The San Francisco Zoo has already welcomed more than 130 additional baby garter snakes in 2026. They are currently being raised in captivity, with another release planned for 2027.Scientists will also monitor the 62 released snakes to understand how well they adapt to their natural surroundings and whether the intervention helps strengthen existing populations. The long-term recovery target is to establish at least 10 viable, self-sustaining breeding populations, each containing a minimum of 200 snakes. Achieving this would help meet the conditions required for the species to be considered for removal from the federal endangered species list.For now, the successful return of 62 zoo-raised snakes marks an important development in a conservation effort that combines scientific research, genetic diversity and habitat protection to give one of California’s rarest reptiles a better chance of survival.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Starshield restrictions help Russia’s energy attacks on Ukraine: Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Starlink has recently denied restricting internet speeds, but Elon Musk suggested the US military could be behind it.
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that speed restrictions by Starlink’s military-grade internet service had aided a wave of deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine.

Two people were killed on Saturday in a Russian drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region.

An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity, Ukraine’s DTEK energy provider said in a Telegram statement.

Ukraine’s army said it shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.

Zelenskyy posted on X that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides commonly attack each other with.

“And many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there,” he posted, citing Starlink’s sister company and reiterating accusations that it was throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations.

The president said on Saturday that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days and that Starlink reported technical problems, but Ukraine does “not believe that is the case”.

It is the second such outage in recent weeks. Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, has denied restricting internet speeds. Last month, Musk said the United States government controls Starshield.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Sunday that it launched attacks targeting Ukraine’s military airfields, munitions depots and other military facilities.

Authorities also said that an electrical engineer was killed and four others were injured in Russia’s Taganrog region after Ukrainian drones attacked the area on Sunday.

Six people were injured in a drone attack in Nizhnekamsk, local officials said. The city, as well as the wider Trans-Kama region of Tatarstan, reported heavy Ukrainian attacks on industrial facilities and a residential building earlier on Sunday.

US negotiators concluded visits to both countries in recent days in attempts to secure a ceasefire, despite tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Zelenskyy said the US floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership .

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin is due to meet President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week – but Ukraine is not on the agenda. Analysts have compared the meeting to the Yalta conference of 1945, which saw the US, UK and former Soviet Union divide Germany and establish the United Nations.

However, in a statement on Sunday, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, dismissed Russia’s longstanding proposal to revise Europe’s security architecture.

“Putin is throwing around ideas about reshaping the European security order. In his dreams, he sees himself in Yalta in 1945. The problem is that to put forward ideas of this magnitude, you first need to win a world war,” he said.

articles.title: ‘Almost magic’ as SpaceX craft caught mid-air: Why it matters
articles.summary: SpaceX’s Starship successfully returned to its launchpad after orbiting in space.
articles.body:
On a cloudy Saturday afternoon in the southern US state of Texas, a pair of large metallic arms stretched out and caught a giant in midair as it descended from the sky.

At 124 metres (407ft) tall, SpaceX’s Starship is the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, intended for travel to the Moon and Mars. Yet 22 hours after its latest blast off into space, it made history on Earth while returning, as it slipped smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 at Starbase city in Texas.

Aerospace engineers across the globe have lauded the first-ever capture of the upper stage of a spaceship and welcomed the achievement, which signals that mega rockets could soon be fully reusable.

Here’s why the historic capture matters:

On Saturday, after orbiting Earth 14 times for 22.5 hours, SpaceX’s Starship emerged from thick clouds over its Starbase launch site, flipped itself to a vertical position and slowly descended into the arms on the ‘Mechazilla’ launch tower.

Like massive tweezers, the arms caught the upper stage of the spacecraft in midair, while its engines were still roaring.

The spacecraft then hooked onto the tower’s mechanical arms and shut off its engines.

The roaring sound was instantly replaced by loud cheers from watchers nearby – they had just seen for the first time in history the capture of a mega rocket.

“That was the missing link, the holy grail of spaceflight,” said SpaceX mission commentator Dan Huot. “We caught a Starship and now everything changes.”

“Congratulations to an incredible team at SpaceX!!!” SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said.

NASA, which is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land astronauts on the Moon later this decade, also welcomed the achievement.

“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on X.

“Making more believers by the day…one step closer to [the moon],” he added.

Spacecraft returning to Earth battle gravity and a range of atmospheric factors that are nearly impossible to perfectly predict or game.

Sputnik 1, the first-ever artificial satellite sent into space, burned up while returning to Earth.

Several manned spacecraft have been destroyed while re-entering the atmosphere, killing the astronauts on board.

In April 1967, the Soviet Union’s Soyuz 1 spacecraft re-entered the atmosphere successfully, but its parachutes failed to deploy properly. Cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov died in the crash-landing near the Ural mountains. Decades later, NASA’s space shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry from orbit, killing all seven astronauts on board.

In recent decades, space agencies and private firms have made major advances in safety. But many spacecraft are impossible to reuse after splashing down in the sea or on land.

Since October 2024, SpaceX has on three occasions successfully caught the boosters that propel shuttles, once they have run out of fuel and separated from the main rocket.

But until now, the main spacecraft has never been successfully caught in midair.

Soon after its return, Musk and his engineers inspected the spaceship and said that everything appeared to have worked well, including its vital heat shield.

“Ship 42 looks great!” Musk wrote on X, posting photos and videos from the launch tower.

While the capture was tricky, aerospace engineers said the upper stage catch is a big success for SpaceX.

Niharika Patel, Technical Programme Manager at Loft Orbital, a US-based space infrastructure company, told Al Jazeera that watching the catch happen was “magical.”

“Landing a rocket back on Earth is incredibly difficult and can itself be considered an engineering marvel. Now add the sheer size and weight of Starship to that equation,” she said, noting that this is also the first time the upper stage booster has been successfully caught.

“It requires incredible precision to ensure the vehicle reaches exactly the right position, withstands the extreme heat of atmospheric re-entry and executes highly controlled manoeuvres within a very tight window. And all of this happens without a pilot — it’s completely autonomous,” she added.

Why does it matter for space technology advances?

SpaceX has become dominant in the aerospace industry primarily because the company has been trying to slash the cost of space travel by launching reusable rocket technology and rapid, repeat engineering.

So far, its Falcon 9 rocket has launched 700 times since 2010, with its first stage being reusable and its second stage discarded into the sea.

With Starship, Musk has said he wants to create fully reusable flights that can also transport humans into space with minimum refurbishment.

“SpaceX has already significantly reduced the cost of getting to orbit through Falcon 9’s reusability. It’s super cheap and convenient to send satellites to low Earth orbit. Starship takes this a step further by being a much bigger craft and aiming for full reusability of both the booster and the upper stage,” Patel said.

She explained that a fully reusable vehicle can be rapidly refurbished and flown again, dramatically increasing frequency and reducing cost. So if Starship reaches this milestone, Patel said it would make access to space even more affordable and scalable, just as commercial aviation transformed travel by making aircraft reusable with quick turnaround times between flights.

“This is essential for the next era of space exploration, from deploying large satellite constellations and building space infrastructure to enabling sustained human exploration of the Moon and Mars,” Patel added.

images.caption: A historic catch - Starship returns to the launchpad in Starbase, Texas [Steve Nesius/Reuters]

articles.title: Archaeologists digging in Beijing have found the first Great Wall remains from the Sui dynasty in the area, a 1,400-year-old frontier outpost with weapons and pottery, plus three wooden boats about 1,800 years old
articles.summary: Archaeologists working in Beijing have uncovered the first confirmed remains of a Sui Dynasty section of the Great Wall in the Chinese capital.
articles.body: Archaeologists working in Beijing have uncovered the first confirmed remains of a Sui Dynasty section of the Great Wall in the Chinese capital. The discovery, made at the Dalinggou site in Changping district, is reshaping what researchers understand about the earliest defences around ancient Beijing. Alongside it, archaeologists have revealed three wooden boats about 1,800 years old, offering an unusually vivid picture of life, trade and transport in the region long before it became a modern metropolis.The Great Wall is often imagined as one vast, unbroken barrier. In reality, it was a shifting network of walls, watchtowers, garrisons and roads built, repaired and expanded by different states over many centuries. The new find matters because it adds a missing piece to that story: evidence that the Sui Dynasty, which ruled from 581 to 618, maintained a military presence on Beijing’s northern edge.A frontier outpost comes into viewThe excavation took place between August and October 2026, covering roughly 800 square-metres at Dalinggou in Changping. Archaeologists from the Beijing Institute of Archaeology uncovered the remains of a military outpost built against an early section of the Great Wall. Its northern wall was incorporated into the existing wall structure, while inside the enclosure were traces of buildings and retaining walls.The walls were made largely from roughly hewn stones bound and filled with loess, with an earth-and-stone core. It is a very different approach from the polished brickwork and sophisticated masonry associated with the much later Ming Dynasty wall. These older remains remind us that the Great Wall was a succession of practical frontier systems adapted to the needs and resources of their time.More than 60 artefacts were recovered from the site, including pottery, porcelain, metal objects, architectural components, everyday items and weapons. Together, they suggest that this was a working military installation, where soldiers, builders and support personnel lived, stored equipment and helped guard a strategically important northern route.Why the Sui discovery mattersBefore this excavation, the Dalinggou site had been classified as part of the Great Wall built during the Northern Qi Dynasty, which ruled from 550 to 577. The new evidence shows that the fortification was also used during the Sui Dynasty, and that parts of it remained in service centuries later, during the Jin Dynasty from 1115 to 1234.Two finds were especially important in dating the site. Archaeologists recovered a Sui-era wuzhu coin, a bronze cash coin with clear value for establishing chronology. They also found a piece of porcelain whose form and manufacturing technique closely resemble known Sui Dynasty ceramics. Individually, such objects might seem small; together, they provide strong evidence that the outpost was active during the Sui period.“This is the first discovery of Sui Dynasty Great Wall remains in the Beijing area,” said Shang Heng, an archaeologist at the Beijing Institute of Archaeology. He explained that the find is valuable for studying the age, location, direction and military defence system of the early Great Wall around Beijing. It may also help researchers trace Sui-era wall sections in neighbouring Hebei and Shanxi provinces.The discovery is particularly significant because the Sui Dynasty was short but transformative. It reunited much of China after centuries of division and laid foundations later inherited by the Tang Dynasty. Its rulers also invested heavily in securing the northern frontier, where the empire faced pressure from peoples beyond its borders. The Beijing find suggests that the Sui did not simply build new defences from nothing; it likely reused and maintained parts of the earlier Northern Qi system.A wall with a longer memoryThe site’s layered history is one of its most compelling features. A fortification first associated with the Northern Qi was later used by the Sui and still showed evidence of activity during the Jin Dynasty. That means the same landscape may have served very different rulers across more than five centuries.This challenges the popular image of the Great Wall as a static monument. Walls were not only built; they were repaired, redirected, garrisoned, abandoned and sometimes absorbed into newer defensive systems. Dalinggou offers a rare chance to see that process in one place, through its architecture and the objects left behind by the people who used it.The discovery also gives archaeologists a geographical reference point. Dalinggou lies along the same defensive line as previously identified Sui-era remains in Hebei and Shanxi. To the west, an inscription in Kelan County, Shanxi, records construction of the Great Wall in 599. To the east, another inscription from 597 was found in Luanping County, Hebei, while a Sui Dynasty beacon tower has been identified in Qianxi County.Put together, these clues suggest a broad frontier network rather than isolated local fortifications. The Beijing discovery could therefore help scholars map the route of the early wall more accurately and understand how military authority was organised across northern China.Three boats beneath BeijingThe announcement also included an equally striking discovery from Fengtai district: three ancient wooden boats, buried about seven metres underground in an old river channel. Known as Yongding River No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3, they date to roughly 1,800 years ago, during the Han and Jin dynasties.These are considered the largest and most structurally complete inland waterway vessels of their period found in northern China. Their discovery provides rare physical evidence that Beijing once had a significant inland transport network, capable of supporting official shipping and movement of goods.One boat bears the Chinese character guan, meaning official. That small mark may indicate that the vessel was built or operated under government authority. The boats also contained a sophisticated system of beams, bottom supports, vertical braces and partition boards, showing considerable skill in early Chinese shipbuilding.Archaeologists found wooden objects, woven matting and human remains associated with the vessels, along with animal bones nearby. The evidence has led researchers to a preliminary interpretation: the boats may have been damaged and gathered at a bend in the river for repair before a sudden flood buried them.What the finds revealTogether, the wall outpost and the boats paint a richer picture of early Beijing. One discovery speaks to the city’s role as a fortified frontier; the other reveals it as a place connected by rivers, transport and trade. Long before skyscrapers and highways, this was a landscape of soldiers, builders, boatmen and communities moving goods along waterways.The Great Wall remains may help explain how empires defended their northern border. The boats may reveal how people and materials moved through it. Both discoveries remind us that history is not only preserved in grand monuments. Sometimes, it survives in a coin, a shard of celadon, a timber joint, or the outline of a wall beneath a modern district.As excavation and analysis continue, Dalinggou and the Yongding River boats are likely to become important reference points for understanding Beijing’s ancient past. They show that the capital’s history extends far beyond its famous later landmarks, reaching back to an age when its fate was tied to frontier defence, river transport and the ambitions of early Chinese empires.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Beavers reintroduced to an English estate changed its stream within a year: Researchers found more land insects, higher oxygen levels and nitrate nearly disappearing downstream, with effects extending at least 1km
articles.summary: Who knew one animal could change an entire landscape?
articles.body: Who knew one animal could change an entire landscape?Beavers in an English estate did not hold meetings about biodiversity, draw up restoration blueprints or worry about water quality. They simply got to work, felling trees, building dams and creating homes around the waterways they inhabit.A recent study in England by University of Liverpool has found that reintroducing beavers to an estate in Essex transformed the surrounding stream in just a year. Researchers recorded an increase in terrestrial insects, higher oxygen levels in the water and a striking reduction in nitrate concentrations downstream. Some of these changes could be detected at least a kilometre away from the beavers' dams.The findings offer another reason to reconsider an animal that was once hunted out of Britain. They also demonstrate how restoring a species can have consequences that extend well beyond the animal itself.A landscape shaped by its inhabitantsThe animals in question are Eurasian beavers (Castor fiber), a species native to Britain that had been hunted to extinction in England around 400 years ago. Their thick fur, meat and castoreum, a substance produced by their scent glands and historically used in perfumes and medicines, made them valuable to hunters. But removing beavers also meant removing an important part of the country's natural ecosystem.Beavers are often described as ecosystem engineers. Unlike animals that simply adapt to their surroundings, they actively change them. They fell trees with their powerful front teeth, construct dams using branches, mud and vegetation, and create ponds that allow them to move through water more safely. These structures slow the movement of streams, allowing water to spread into surrounding areas and form wetlands.What might look like a rather inconvenient obstruction to a flowing stream can become an entirely new habitat for wildlife. Ponds, muddy banks, fallen trees and waterlogged vegetation offer different living conditions for insects, amphibians, birds and aquatic organisms. Even the trees felled by beavers have a second purpose, providing deadwood that supports insects and fungi.It is this ability to change the conditions around them that makes beavers particularly interesting to conservationists. Rather than simply introducing another species into an ecosystem, bringing back beavers can help restore some of the natural processes that disappeared alongside them.What happened at Spains Hall Estate?Researchers from the University of Oxford and the University of Essex, including Oliver John Sworder and Michelle Jackson, studied the effects of reintroducing beavers to enclosures at Spains Hall Estate in Essex.The team collected information about the stream's water quality, algae and invertebrate populations for a year before the beavers arrived in 2023. They then repeated their observations a year after the animals had been introduced. This before-and-after approach offered an opportunity to examine how the ecosystem changed following the reintroduction, rather than relying solely on comparisons between different streams.The findings, published alongside an openly accessible dataset on Dryad on November 3, 2026, showed that the changes were not limited to the immediate area around the dams. One of the most noticeable differences was the increase in terrestrial invertebrates, both in their abundance and species richness. In simpler terms, there were more land-dwelling invertebrates, and researchers recorded a greater variety of them.Insects and other small invertebrates are essential to the functioning of ecosystems. They pollinate plants, break down organic matter, recycle nutrients and provide food for birds, fish, amphibians and other animals. An increase in their numbers can therefore have consequences that travel up the food chain.The researchers also examined freshwater invertebrates, but the findings here were more complicated. There was no statistically significant increase in overall freshwater invertebrate richness, abundance or biomass. However, certain indicator groups were affected, and the composition of feeding groups within the stream changed. In other words, the beavers did not simply make every category of aquatic insect more plentiful. They altered the conditions in which different organisms lived and fed.The surprising effect on water qualityPerhaps the most striking finding concerned the water itself. Researchers recorded an increase in dissolved oxygen throughout the stream following the beavers' arrival. Dissolved oxygen is exactly what it sounds like: oxygen present in water, which aquatic organisms rely on to survive. Fish, insect larvae and other freshwater animals need sufficient oxygen to carry out essential biological processes. When oxygen levels fall too low, aquatic ecosystems can become difficult places to survive.The researchers also examined nitrate concentrations, which offered another interesting result. Nitrate is a naturally occurring form of nitrogen, but excessive amounts entering waterways can become a serious environmental problem. Agricultural fertilisers, animal waste and other sources can introduce additional nitrogen into streams and rivers. When concentrations become too high, they can encourage excessive algae growth. As this algae dies and decomposes, microorganisms consume oxygen in the process, potentially leaving less available for other aquatic life.Here, the researchers noticed something rather unexpected. Nitrate concentrations increased in the water around the beaver dams, but downstream, the nitrate was almost completely filtered out following the reintroduction.Beaver dams can slow water movement, allowing sediment and organic material to settle rather than being carried further downstream. The wetlands they create can also encourage biological processes through which nitrogen is absorbed by vegetation or converted into nitrogen gas by microorganisms. These processes can help remove excess nitrogen from waterways.Although the study does not establish that one particular mechanism was responsible for the changes, the results suggest that beaver activity can influence how nutrients move through an ecosystem.Even more interestingly, the effects were not confined to the immediate surroundings of the dams. Researchers found that the changes extended at least a kilometre downstream. This suggests that the ecological benefits of beaver activity can travel considerably further than the structures the animals build.A little more room for natureThe findings arrive at an interesting time for conservation in Britain. After centuries of absence, beavers are gradually returning to English waterways through managed reintroduction programmes and the expansion of existing populations.In February 2025, the British government announced that wild releases of beavers in England would be permitted under licences issued by Natural England. The decision marked an important step towards restoring a species that once played a natural role in shaping the country's rivers and wetlands.However, bringing back beavers is not without its complications. Their dams can cause localised flooding, affect agricultural land and change the availability of habitats for certain species. Watercourses do not exist in isolation from people, and the interests of farmers, landowners and nearby communities must be considered when deciding where reintroductions should take place. The benefits also depend on the characteristics of individual landscapes, so what works in one location may not necessarily work in another.There is also an important distinction to make about the latest research. The observations were collected over a relatively short period of one year, at a managed estate. They offer encouraging evidence of how quickly ecological changes can begin, but longer-term monitoring will be needed to understand whether these improvements persist and how they develop over time.Still, the study makes a compelling case for looking at conservation differently. Protecting an ecosystem does not always mean intervening in every little detail. Sometimes, it means bringing back the species that already know how to look after it.Beavers build dams because they need deeper water and safer places to live. They fell trees because they need food and building materials. Yet, in meeting their own needs, they create habitats for countless other organisms, alter the movement of water and influence the nutrients flowing through it.A year after their arrival, the stream at Spains Hall Estate was already showing signs of these changes. There were more land-dwelling invertebrates, higher oxygen levels and considerably less nitrate downstream.Perhaps the most encouraging part is that the beavers were not introduced to perform any of these individual tasks. They were simply given a place to live and allowed to do what comes naturally. Sometimes, nature's most effective restoration workers are already there.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Trump moves to build his space legacy with NASA’s help
articles.summary: President Trump is about to do JFK one better.
articles.body:
Lost in the glare of the recent midterms and their startling results, President Trump released a proclamation entitled The American Declaration of Freedom in Space . The document states that American policy will be to open up the solar system “forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty.”

Summoning the legacy of the Apollo moon landings and the ongoing Artemis program, Trump’s proclamation set an ultimate goal for America’s space effort that goes beyond just returning to the moon and going on to Mars.

It states that “the solar system and all of outer space beyond Earth are the province of all humans and are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence by American citizens consistent with United States law and the international obligations of the United States.”

As noted, the proclamation does not set aside the Outer Space Treaty by claiming the solar system for the U.S. as sovereign territory. But it is firm in the principle that the U.S. will lead the winning of the high frontier of space.

A few short years ago, Trump’s proclamation and the vision contained within it would have seemed to be more a scenario of a science fiction story than government policy. Now, the document has been barely remarked on, even by critics. The wide acceptance of the Artemis program and the rise of the commercial space sector, as exemplified by SpaceX and Blue Origin, have made dreams of an interplanetary civilization into a likely future.

Three days after the midterms, President Trump traveled to the Kennedy Space Center in Florida to deliver remarks at Max Power , a technology exhibition and air show. Some of his speech covered the midterms and more Earthly issues. But the heart of what the president had to say celebrated the space program, as well as technological advances such as nuclear power and the Human Genome Project. He noted the upcoming Artemis IV moon landing, with missions scheduled to begin in 2028, the final year of his current and last term in office.

The very next day, NASA announced contracts issued under the next phase of the Commercial Lunar Payload Services program.

“The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on the Moon’s South Pole.”

No matter what happens, Donald Trump will not be president of the United States after Jan. 20, 2029. After the thumping that the Republicans received in the recent midterms, Trump has two things to do. He has to hold the line against emboldened congressional Democrats, and he has to build a lasting legacy.

The first task should be straightforward. Like President Obama after his midterm defeat in 2014, Trump has a veto pen and a phone. He will have to fend off attacks on Elon Musk, the entrepreneur crucial to the spread of human civilization across the solar system.

For the second task, Trump should look to the example of President Reagan after the 1986 midterm elections. Reagan was the subject of endless investigations and threats of impeachment surrounding the Iran-Contra scandal, just as Trump is likely to be because of a multitude of real and perceived sins.

Despite all that, Reagan left office with a 63 percent approval rating . Then, when the Berlin Wall fell, followed by the Soviet Union, he became a world historic figure, mentioned in the same breath as Washington and Lincoln. Incidentally, Reagan’s legacy also includes the orbiting laboratory that eventually became known as the International Space Station.

If all goes as planned, in the midst of the tiresome veto fights and endless investigations, in 2028, American astronauts will walk on the moon. America and the world will stop and watch in wonder at the sight, not seen since Richard Nixon was in office.

No matter what one feels about Trump, hate him or love him, the unalterable fact will be that he set that next moonwalk in motion. The Artemis program has survived changes of administrations and congresses. It is one thing that most Americans, on both sides of the political divide, agree is glorious and good.

Think of President John F. Kennedy. Two things are remembered of him. He was assassinated and he threw down the gauntlet for the race to the moon.

President Trump is about to do Kennedy one better. The Apollo program ended. The Artemis program and what will follow will never end. Not a bad legacy.

Mark R. Whittington, who writes frequently about space policy, has published a political study of space exploration entitled “ Why is It So Hard to Go Back to the Moon? ” as well as “ The Moon, Mars and Beyond ” and, most recently, “ Why is America Going Back to the Moon? ” He blogs at Curmudgeons Corner.
